portal.title: HNCareCompass: Your Patient Portal App
portal.intro: HNCareCompass is Holy Name's free patient portal app. It puts everything you need for your care in one secure place on your phone.

items.t: What you can do in the app
items.h:
• View your medical records
  • See your lab results as soon as they are ready
  • View your prescriptions and request refills
  • Schedule and manage your appointments
  • Make payments

Track and manage your health in one place:

  • Health goals
  • Medications
  • Schedules
  • Lab results
  • Payments
  • Vital signs, such as blood pressure, heart rate, and weight

Search for HNCareCompass in the App Store or Google Play, or tap the link for your phone.

s1.title: Getting Started

items.h:
Your first visit is a chance to get to know your care team and make a plan for a healthy pregnancy.

What to bring or be ready to talk about

  • The first day of your last period. This helps us find your due date.
  • A list of all medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take.
  • Your health history, including any long-term conditions, surgeries, and vaccines.
  • Your pregnancy history, including any miscarriages, stillbirths, abortions, early (preterm) births, preeclampsia, or diabetes during pregnancy.
  • Any questions or concerns you have.

Honest and complete answers help us give you the best care. Your privacy is important to us.

Other questions we may ask

  • Who supports you at home
  • Whether you have enough healthy food
  • How you get to your appointments
  • Anything that makes it hard for you to get care

If you need help with any of these, please tell us. We may be able to connect you with resources.

What to expect at your visit

  • A review of your health, pregnancy, and surgery history
  • A full physical exam, including a Pap test if you are due for one
  • Your due date, with an ultrasound if needed to confirm it
  • A talk about any risks in your pregnancy
  • A plan for your prenatal care
  • Vaccines, if you need them
  • A talk about genetic screening and testing choices
  • Referrals to specialists if you need extra care

Blood and urine tests

Routine lab tests at the first visit may include:

  • Blood type, Rh factor, and antibody screen
  • Complete blood count (to check for anemia, or low iron)
  • Immunity to rubella (German measles) and varicella (chickenpox)
  • Hepatitis B and hepatitis C
  • HIV and syphilis
  • Chlamydia and gonorrhea
  • Urine test for protein, sugar, and infection
  • Kidney, liver, thyroid, or tuberculosis (TB) tests, if needed
  • Genetic screening for you and your baby, if you choose (see Section 2)

Most pregnancies follow this schedule:

  • Every 4 weeks until 28 weeks
  • Every 2 weeks from 28 to 36 weeks
  • Every week from 36 weeks until your baby is born

If you have concerns or a problem comes up, you may need extra visits. Some patients also see a maternal-fetal medicine (high-risk pregnancy) specialist.

s1.src: Sources: ACOG, Routine Tests During Pregnancy (FAQ); ACOG Practice Advisory, Hepatitis C in Pregnancy: Updated Guidelines (2021); ACOG Practice Advisory, Screening for Syphilis in Pregnancy (2024); ACOG/AAP, Guidelines for Perinatal Care, 8th ed. (visit schedule).

s2.title: Tests During Pregnancy: First and Second Trimester

items.h:
Dating ultrasound

An early ultrasound confirms the pregnancy and checks for a heartbeat. It shows whether there is more than one baby. It also gives the most accurate due date.

First blood and urine tests

The lab tests listed in Section 1 are done at or soon after your first visit.

Carrier screening

This blood test checks whether you carry a gene for certain inherited conditions. Examples are cystic fibrosis, spinal muscular atrophy, and blood disorders such as sickle cell disease. If you are a carrier, your partner can be tested too. You only need this test once in your life. It can be done before or during pregnancy.

Early diabetes screening

Some patients are tested for diabetes at the first visit instead of waiting until 24–28 weeks. This may apply if you have obesity, had diabetes in a past pregnancy, or have a strong family history of diabetes.

Screening for chromosome conditions

Every patient is offered screening for chromosome conditions such as Down syndrome, no matter your age. You can choose a screening test, a diagnostic test, or no test at all.

  • Cell-free DNA screening (NIPT): a blood test that can be done from 10 weeks on. It screens for Down syndrome (trisomy 21), trisomy 18, trisomy 13, and sex chromosome conditions. It is the most accurate screening test for these conditions.
  • First-trimester screening: a blood test plus an ultrasound. The ultrasound measures the fluid at the back of the baby's neck (called nuchal translucency). It is done between 10 and 13 weeks 6 days.
  • Chorionic villus sampling (CVS): a diagnostic test done between 10 and 13 weeks. A small sample of the placenta is tested. It gives a definite answer about chromosome conditions.

Screening blood tests (15–22 weeks)

  • Quad screen: a blood test for Down syndrome, trisomy 18, and spine or brain defects (neural tube defects). It is used if you did not have first-trimester screening or NIPT.
  • AFP blood test: if you had NIPT, a separate blood test for neural tube defects (such as spina bifida) is offered between 15 and 22 weeks. The anatomy ultrasound can also check for these.

Anatomy ultrasound (20 weeks or later)

A detailed ultrasound done at 20 weeks or later. It looks at the baby's organs, brain, spine, heart, arms, and legs. It also checks the placenta and the baby's growth. You can usually learn the baby's sex if you want to know. Some patients have an earlier "early anatomy" ultrasound; this does not replace the 20-week scan.

Amniocentesis (16 weeks or later)

A diagnostic test done at 16 weeks or later. A thin needle removes a small amount of the fluid around the baby. The baby's chromosomes are tested directly. It is offered to anyone who wants a definite answer, or after a positive screening test.

Glucose test for diabetes (24–28 weeks)

This test checks for gestational diabetes (diabetes that starts during pregnancy).

  • You drink a sweet drink. Your blood is drawn one hour later.
  • You do not need to fast. The visit takes about one hour.
  • If the result is high, you will have a longer 3-hour test to confirm it.

Repeat blood count (24–28 weeks)

Your blood count is checked again for anemia (low iron). Anemia is common in the second half of pregnancy.

Rh-negative blood type (28 weeks)

If your blood type is Rh negative, you get a shot called Rh immune globulin (RhoGAM) at about 28 weeks. You get another shot after birth if your baby is Rh positive. This protects future pregnancies.

s2.src: Sources: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 226, Screening for Fetal Chromosomal Abnormalities (2020); ACOG Committee Opinions No. 690 and 691, Carrier Screening (2017); ACOG Committee Opinion No. 700, Methods for Estimating the Due Date (2017); ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 190, Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (2018); ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 233, Anemia in Pregnancy (2021); ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 181, Prevention of Rh D Alloimmunization (2017); ACOG, Prenatal Genetic Screening Tests and Prenatal Genetic Diagnostic Tests (FAQs).

s2.title: Tests During Pregnancy: Third Trimester and Vaccines

items.h:
Group B strep (GBS) test (36–37 weeks)

  • A quick swab of the vagina and rectum is done in the office. It is done between 36 weeks 0 days and 37 weeks 6 days.
  • GBS is a common germ. It is harmless for most adults. But it can cause a serious infection in a newborn.
  • If your test is positive, you will get antibiotics through an IV during labor. This protects your baby.

More blood tests

In the third trimester, you will also have blood tests to:

  • Check for anemia (low iron)
  • Check again for HIV and syphilis. ACOG recommends a repeat syphilis test in the third trimester and at delivery. New Jersey law requires HIV and syphilis testing in the third trimester.

Checking on your baby

Depending on your health and your baby's growth, your provider may order extra ultrasounds or heart-rate monitoring (non-stress tests) in the third trimester.

If you have questions about any of these tests or vaccines, your provider will be happy to talk with you.

Depending on your health history and how far along you are, your provider will recommend:

  • Tdap (whooping cough): in every pregnancy, between 27 and 36 weeks. Earlier in that window is best. It protects your newborn from whooping cough.
  • Flu shot: during flu season, in any trimester. Pregnant patients get the shot, not the nasal spray.
  • RSV vaccine: one dose between 32 and 36 weeks 6 days, given September through January. It protects your newborn from severe RSV lung infection. If you do not get it, your baby can get an RSV antibody shot after birth.
  • COVID-19 vaccine: recommended and safe in any trimester.
  • Rh immune globulin (RhoGAM): at about 28 weeks if your blood type is Rh negative. This is not a vaccine, but it is given on the same schedule.

Live vaccines (MMR and chickenpox) are not given during pregnancy. If you are not immune to rubella or chickenpox, you will get these vaccines after your baby is born.

s2.src: Sources: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 797, Prevention of Group B Streptococcal Early-Onset Disease in Newborns (2020); ACOG Practice Advisory, Screening for Syphilis in Pregnancy (2024); New Jersey prenatal HIV and syphilis testing statutes; ACOG Committee Opinion No. 718, Tdap Vaccination (2017); ACOG Committee Opinion No. 732, Influenza Vaccination During Pregnancy (2018); ACOG Practice Advisory, Maternal Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccination (2023, updated 2024); ACOG Practice Advisory, COVID-19 Vaccination Considerations for Obstetric–Gynecologic Care; ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 181 (2017).

s2.title: Genetic Screening and Testing: What Is the Difference?

items.h:
Chromosomes carry our genes. Most babies have 46 chromosomes. Sometimes a baby has an extra chromosome or is missing one. This is called aneuploidy. Some chromosome conditions cause miscarriage. Others affect a baby's health and development. Examples include:

  • Down syndrome (trisomy 21)
  • Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18)
  • Patau syndrome (trisomy 13)
  • Turner syndrome (monosomy X)

NIPT, first-trimester screening, and the quad screen are screening tests. They tell you whether your baby has a higher or lower chance of a condition. They cannot tell you for sure. A positive screening result should be confirmed with a diagnostic test before any decisions are made.

CVS and amniocentesis take cells from the placenta or the fluid around the baby. The baby's chromosomes are tested directly. These are diagnostic tests because they give a definite answer. They carry a small risk of miscarriage. Your provider will talk with you about this.

Being a carrier usually does not mean you have the condition or are sick. It means you carry a gene for the condition and could pass it to your baby. If both parents carry a gene for the same condition, there is a chance the baby could have it. Both parents can be tested to find out.

Talk with your provider about which tests, if any, are right for you. Genetic counseling is available. Testing is always your choice.

s2.src: Sources: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 226 (2020); ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 162, Prenatal Diagnostic Testing for Genetic Disorders (2016); ACOG Committee Opinion No. 690 (2017).

s3.title: Food and Daily Life

items.h:
A balanced diet gives you and your baby most of what you need. Eat fruits, vegetables, whole grains, dairy (or calcium-rich foods), and protein. A daily prenatal vitamin fills in the gaps. Key daily amounts during pregnancy:

NutrientDaily amountWhy it matters
Folic acid600 micrograms (400 before pregnancy)Prevents spine and brain defects. Take a supplement; diet alone is not enough.
Iron27 mgPrevents anemia (low iron) and supports the baby's blood supply
Calcium1,000 mg (1,300 mg if age 18 or younger)Bones and teeth. Most prenatal vitamins have only 200–300 mg, so eat calcium-rich foods.
Vitamin D600 international unitsBone health; helps the body use calcium
Choline450 mgBrain and spinal cord development
Iodine220 microgramsThyroid and brain development

If a past pregnancy had a neural tube defect, you need a higher folic acid dose (4 mg a day). Ask your provider. ACOG does not recommend routine vitamin D blood tests or extra vitamin D beyond a standard prenatal vitamin.

How much weight to gain depends on your body mass index (BMI) before pregnancy. Most people need only about 340 extra calories a day in the second trimester and 450 in the third. You do not need extra calories in the first trimester.

BMI before pregnancyRecommended total gain
Underweight (below 18.5)28–40 pounds
Normal weight (18.5–24.9)25–35 pounds
Overweight (25–29.9)15–25 pounds
Obesity (30 or higher)11–20 pounds

These ranges are a general guide. Your provider will tailor them to you.

items.t: How Much Water Should I Drink?
items.h: Drink 8–12 cups (64–96 ounces) of water every day. Water helps your baby grow, forms the fluid around your baby, helps digestion, prevents constipation, and carries nutrients through your body. Drink more if you exercise, are in hot weather, or feel thirsty.

Yes. Keep caffeine under 200 mg a day. That is about one 12-ounce cup of coffee. This amount has not been linked to miscarriage or early birth. Caffeine is also in tea, chocolate, energy drinks, and soda. Count all sources.

Aspartame, sucralose, acesulfame potassium, and stevia have not been shown to cause birth defects. They may be used in moderation. There is less information on saccharin, but small amounts are likely safe.

There is no known safe amount of alcohol during pregnancy, and no safe time to drink. Alcohol can cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorders. These cause lifelong physical, behavior, and learning problems. If you are pregnant or trying to get pregnant, do not drink alcohol. If it is hard to stop, tell your provider. Confidential help is available.

• Smoking raises the risk of miscarriage, placenta problems, early birth, low birth weight, birth defects, and stillbirth. Quitting at any time in pregnancy helps you and your baby.
  • Nicotine patches or gum may be an option after counseling, with your provider's guidance. Ask about the New Jersey Quitline: 1-866-NJ-QUITS.
  • E-cigarettes and vaping are not safe in pregnancy. They are not recommended as a way to quit.
  • Stay away from secondhand smoke.

Do not use marijuana during pregnancy or while breastfeeding. It may affect your baby's brain development. No safe amount is known. This includes smoking, vaping, and edibles. Do not use marijuana for nausea. Safe treatments are available (see Section 5).

s3.src: Sources: ACOG, Nutrition During Pregnancy (FAQ); ACOG Committee Opinion No. 548, Weight Gain During Pregnancy (2013, reaffirmed); ACOG Committee Opinion No. 495, Vitamin D (2011, reaffirmed); ACOG Committee Opinion No. 462, Moderate Caffeine Consumption During Pregnancy (2010, reaffirmed); ACOG Committee Opinion No. 496, At-Risk Drinking and Alcohol Dependence (2011, reaffirmed) and ACOG, Tobacco, Alcohol, Drugs, and Pregnancy (FAQ); ACOG Committee Opinion No. 807, Tobacco and Nicotine Cessation During Pregnancy (2020); ACOG Committee Opinion No. 722, Marijuana Use During Pregnancy and Lactation (2017). Artificial sweeteners: Fox NS, Obstet Gynecol 2018 (not addressed in ACOG guidance).

s3.title: Fish and Food Safety

items.t: Fish: Eat It, and Choose Wisely
items.h:
Fish is a great source of protein and omega-3 fats (DHA). These help your baby's brain and eyes develop. ACOG recommends 2–3 servings (8–12 ounces) a week of fish that is low in mercury.

Good choices (low mercury)

Salmon, sardines, anchovies, herring, trout, tilapia, cod, pollock, catfish, shrimp, canned light tuna, and other shellfish.

Limit

White (albacore) tuna: no more than 6 ounces a week.

Avoid (high mercury)

King mackerel, shark, swordfish, tilefish, marlin, orange roughy, and bigeye tuna.

Do not eat raw or undercooked fish or shellfish during pregnancy. This includes sushi and sashimi made with raw fish, raw oysters, and raw clams. Raw fish can carry germs or parasites that can make you sick. Fully cooked fish is safe. Sushi made with cooked fish or vegetables is safe too.

Listeria is a germ found in some foods. It can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, or a serious infection in a newborn. Pregnant women are much more likely than others to get sick from it. Toxoplasmosis is a parasite found in undercooked meat, unwashed produce, soil, and cat litter. To lower your risk:

  • Do not drink raw (unpasteurized) milk. Do not eat soft cheeses made from it, such as some queso fresco, feta, Brie, Camembert, and blue cheese. Check the label for "made with pasteurized milk."
  • Do not eat hot dogs, deli meats, or cold cuts unless they are heated until steaming hot.
  • Avoid refrigerated pâté, meat spreads, and refrigerated smoked seafood unless they are cooked in a dish.
  • Avoid raw sprouts. Wash all fruits and vegetables well.
  • Cook meat, poultry, eggs, and seafood all the way through. Avoid raw or undercooked meat and eggs, including raw cookie dough.
  • Wear gloves when gardening. If you can, have someone else change the cat litter. If you must do it, wear gloves and wash your hands after.
  • Wash your hands, utensils, and counters after handling raw meat.
  • Watch for food recalls for Listeria. Throw out recalled foods.

Call your provider if you have a fever, muscle aches, or flu-like symptoms after eating a food you are worried about. Listeria infection can be treated with antibiotics.

s3.src: Sources: ACOG, Nutrition During Pregnancy (FAQ); U.S. FDA/EPA, Advice About Eating Fish (as adopted in ACOG guidance); ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 151, Cytomegalovirus, Parvovirus B19, Varicella Zoster, and Toxoplasmosis in Pregnancy (2015, reaffirmed); Fox NS, Obstet Gynecol 2018 (Listeria recall guidance). Where Fox NS and ACOG differ (sushi from reputable establishments), ACOG guidance is followed.

s4.title: Exercise During Pregnancy

items.h:
Yes. We encourage most patients to stay active during pregnancy. Exercise can help you feel better, get your body ready for labor, and help you recover after birth.

How much?

  • Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise each week. That is about 30 minutes, 5 days a week.
  • "Moderate" means your heart beats faster and you may sweat. You can still talk, but you cannot sing.
  • If you are new to exercise, start with 5–10 minutes a day. Add more slowly.

Regular exercise can:

  • Reduce back pain
  • Ease constipation
  • Lower the risk of gestational diabetes, preeclampsia, and cesarean birth
  • Help you gain a healthy amount of weight
  • Improve your overall fitness and heart health
  • Help you lose the baby weight after delivery

Safe activities

  • Walking
  • Swimming and water exercise
  • Stationary bike
  • Prenatal yoga and modified Pilates
  • Running, jogging, racquet sports, and strength training, if you did them before pregnancy. Talk with your provider first.

• Contact sports (soccer, basketball, boxing, ice hockey)
  • Activities where you could fall (downhill skiing, water skiing, surfing, off-road biking, gymnastics, horseback riding)
  • Hot yoga or hot Pilates
  • Scuba diving
  • Skydiving
  • Exercise above 6,000 feet, unless you already live at that altitude

Exercise tips

  • Drink water before, during, and after exercise.
  • Wear a supportive sports bra. A belly-support belt may help later in pregnancy.
  • Do not get overheated. Exercise in a cool, well-ventilated space. Skip outdoor exercise on very hot, humid days.
  • After the first trimester, avoid exercises where you lie flat on your back for a long time.

items.t: Stop exercising and call your provider if you have
items.h:
• Bleeding from the vagina
  • Fluid leaking from the vagina
  • Regular, painful contractions
  • Dizziness or feeling faint
  • Shortness of breath before you start exercising
  • Chest pain
  • Headache
  • Muscle weakness that affects your balance
  • Calf pain or swelling

Some conditions change what is safe. Examples are certain heart or lung conditions, placenta previa after 26 weeks, preeclampsia, severe anemia, and risk of early labor. If any of these apply to you, talk with your provider about what activities are safe.

Bed rest has not been shown to prevent early birth or miscarriage. It can cause harm, such as blood clots, muscle loss, and stress. It is not routinely recommended. If a problem comes up, your provider will tell you what level of activity is right for you.

s4.src: Sources: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 804, Physical Activity and Exercise During Pregnancy and the Postpartum Period (2020); ACOG, Exercise During Pregnancy (FAQ); Fox NS, Obstet Gynecol 2018 (bed rest).

s4.title: Common Questions

items.h:
Sex is safe throughout pregnancy as long as it is comfortable and your provider has not told you to avoid it. Your provider may tell you to avoid sex if you have placenta previa, preterm labor, bleeding, or your water has broken.

Mild cramping after sex or orgasm is normal. Light spotting after sex is also normal.

Call your OB-GYN if you have strong or lasting cramps, or heavy bleeding like a period.

After your baby is born, wait until you have healed and feel ready. You will talk about timing at your postpartum visit. Talk about birth control before then. You can get pregnant again before your first period.

Whether to have sex during pregnancy is your choice. Do what feels comfortable for you.

items.t: Should I go to the dentist?
items.h:
Healthy teeth and gums are part of a healthy pregnancy.

  • Keep your routine dental cleanings and exams.
  • Dental X-rays are safe when needed. A lead apron over your belly and a thyroid collar are used.
  • Do not put off needed dental work (fillings, extractions, root canals) because you are pregnant.
  • Numbing medicine (local anesthetic, such as lidocaine) is safe.
  • Tell your dentist you are pregnant before any treatment.

Hair dye is considered safe during pregnancy. Only a very small amount of the chemicals is absorbed through your scalp. There is no evidence it harms your baby. This applies to permanent, semi-permanent, and temporary dye. Use it in a room with good airflow, wear gloves if you apply it yourself, and follow the directions.

Avoid anything that raises your body temperature too much. Hot tub use has been linked to a higher risk of miscarriage, especially in the first trimester. Avoid hot tubs and saunas in early pregnancy. Swimming in a pool is safe and is a great form of exercise.
EPA-registered insect repellents, including DEET and picaridin, are safe in pregnancy. Use them where mosquitoes carry illness (such as West Nile or Zika virus). Follow the label.

Travel is usually safe if you do not have a high-risk condition. Talk with your provider before you make plans. The most comfortable time to travel is often between 14 and 28 weeks. By then nausea has usually eased and your energy is better. There is no exact week when travel must stop. As pregnancy goes on, weigh the benefit of the trip against the chance of a problem away from home.

Before you travel

  • Check the CDC travel website for health concerns (including Zika) where you are going.
  • Find the nearest hospital where you will be staying. Bring a copy of your prenatal record.
  • Wash your hands often. Carry hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol for when you cannot wash.

By car

  • Take the shortest route. Stop every 1–2 hours to walk and stretch.
  • Always wear your seat belt. Put the lap belt low across your hips, under your belly. Put the shoulder belt between your breasts and to the side of your belly. Never put the lap belt over your belly.
  • Keep the airbags on. Move your seat back as far as is comfortable.

By plane

  • Flying is safe in a healthy pregnancy. Most U.S. airlines allow travel until about 36 weeks. International flights may have earlier limits. Check your airline's policy before you book.
  • Choose an aisle seat. Keep your seat belt fastened under your belly. Drink plenty of water. Walk the aisle or stretch your legs at least once an hour to lower the risk of blood clots.
  • Compression (support) stockings may help with swelling on longer flights.

s4.src: Sources: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 736, Optimizing Postpartum Care (2018); ACOG Committee Opinion No. 569, Oral Health Care During and After Pregnancy (2013, reaffirmed); ACOG patient education, Your Pregnancy and Childbirth: Month to Month, 7th ed. (hair dye) and Fox NS, Obstet Gynecol 2018; ACOG Committee Opinion No. 804 (overheating); ACOG/SMFM Practice Advisory on Zika Virus (insect repellent); ACOG, Travel During Pregnancy (FAQ); ACOG Committee Opinion No. 746, Air Travel During Pregnancy (2018); Fox NS, Obstet Gynecol 2018 (hot tubs; no fixed week limit for travel); CDC, Hand Hygiene (hand sanitizer).

s5.title: Common Symptoms

items.h:
Nausea and vomiting are very common, especially in the first trimester. Despite the name, "morning sickness" can happen at any time of day. It usually does not harm your baby. But it can make it hard to eat, drink, work, or enjoy your day. Safe treatments are available. Treating it early keeps it from getting worse.

Tips to ease nausea

  • Eat a few crackers or dry toast before you get out of bed.
  • Eat small meals often so your stomach is never empty. Snack on crackers, nuts, or fruit.
  • Try bland foods: bananas, rice, applesauce, toast, and tea (the BRAT diet).
  • Add protein to meals and snacks: yogurt, milk, nuts, nut butter, protein shakes.
  • Avoid spicy, greasy, fried, or fatty foods. Avoid smells that make you feel sick.
  • Sip fluids all day. Cold or sour drinks may go down easier.
  • Take your prenatal vitamin at bedtime or with a snack. If it makes nausea worse, ask about taking folic acid alone until you feel better.

Ginger may help

Try ginger tea, ginger candies, ginger capsules (250 mg up to 4 times a day), or ginger ale made with real ginger.

Vitamins and medicines

  • Vitamin B6 can ease nausea. It works best with doxylamine, an over-the-counter sleep aid. This combination is the first medicine ACOG recommends. See Section 6 for doses.
  • Acupressure wristbands or acupuncture help some people.
  • If these are not enough, your provider can prescribe a safe anti-nausea medicine.

Call your provider if

  • You cannot keep liquids down
  • You urinate very little, or your urine is dark yellow
  • You feel dizzy or faint when you stand
  • Your heart is racing or pounding
  • You are losing weight

Heartburn is very common in pregnancy. It comes from normal hormone and body changes.

  • Eat smaller meals more often.
  • Avoid foods that set it off: tomato foods, citrus fruit and juice, coffee and caffeine, and spicy or greasy foods.
  • Do not lie down for 2–3 hours after eating.
  • Raise the head of your bed, or use extra pillows, if heartburn is worse at night.

Antacids such as Tums are safe in pregnancy. If heartburn is frequent or severe, ask your provider about other safe medicines (see Section 6).

Hemorrhoids are swollen veins around the anus. They are common in pregnancy. Pressure from the growing uterus and constipation cause them. They can cause pain, itching, and bleeding when you have a bowel movement.

  • Eat high-fiber foods and drink plenty of water to prevent constipation.
  • Stay active. Do not sit for long periods.
  • Gain weight in the range your provider recommends.
  • Use an ice pack or witch hazel pads to ease pain and swelling.
  • Soak in a warm (not hot) bath or sitz bath several times a day.
  • Over-the-counter hemorrhoid creams may help. Ask your provider.

Call your provider if

  • You have heavy or ongoing bleeding from the rectum
  • Your pain is severe or does not get better with home care
  • You have a painful lump that becomes very swollen or hard

s5.src: Sources: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 189, Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy (2018); ACOG, Morning Sickness: Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy (FAQ); ACOG, Problems of the Digestive System (FAQ).

s5.title: Common Symptoms

items.h:
Pregnancy hormones slow down your digestion. Iron pills can make constipation worse.

  • Eat about 25 grams of fiber each day. Good sources: fruits (apples, bananas, raspberries), vegetables, whole grains, beans, lentils, nuts, and seeds. Add fiber slowly to avoid gas and bloating.
  • Drink plenty of water. Stay active if your provider says it is safe.
  • If that is not enough, fiber supplements, stool softeners such as Colace, and MiraLAX are safe in pregnancy (see Section 6). Tell your provider if constipation is severe or does not get better.

Back pain is very common, especially later in pregnancy. As your uterus grows, your center of gravity shifts forward and your belly muscles stretch and weaken. This changes your posture and strains your back. Extra weight adds to the load. Back pain usually gets better after your baby is born.

  • Wear low-heeled (but not flat) shoes with good arch support. Do not wear high heels. They tilt your body forward and strain your lower back.
  • Sit in chairs with good back support, or tuck a small pillow behind your lower back.
  • To lift, squat down, bend your knees, and keep your back straight. Do not bend at the waist. Avoid lifting heavy things.
  • If you must stand for a long time, rest one foot on a small stool or box.
  • Sleep on your side with one or both knees bent. Put a pillow between your knees and another under your belly.
  • Use a heating pad on the lowest setting, wrapped in a towel, or a cold pack. Do not use either for a long time.
  • A maternity support belt or garment can help carry the weight of your belly.
  • Stay active. Walking and water exercise are good choices. Exercises that strengthen your back and belly muscles can ease pain. Ask your provider which exercises are safe for you.

Call your provider if

  • Your back pain is severe
  • The pain lasts more than 2 weeks
  • You also have fever, burning when you urinate, bleeding, contractions, or leaking fluid. These can be signs of a urinary tract infection or preterm labor.
Read ACOG's patient guide, Back Pain During Pregnancy
acog.org/womens-health/faqs/back-pain-during-pregnancy
↗

items.t: Swelling in the Legs and Feet
items.h:
Mild swelling of the feet and ankles is normal, especially late in pregnancy and at the end of the day.

  • Do not stand or sit in one position for a long time. Put your feet up whenever you can.
  • Stay active with walking or other exercise your provider approves.
  • Wear comfortable shoes. Compression stockings may help. Drink plenty of water.

Call your provider right away if

  • Swelling starts suddenly or becomes severe
  • One leg is more swollen than the other, especially with pain, redness, warmth, or tenderness
  • Swelling comes with a headache that will not go away, vision changes, pain in the upper belly, nausea, or swelling of the face or hands. These can be signs of preeclampsia.
  • You have chest pain, a racing heart, or trouble breathing: get emergency care

• Drink plenty of water and eat regular, balanced meals.
  • Rest in a quiet, dark room. Keep a regular sleep schedule. Avoid things that trigger your headaches.
  • Put a cool cloth on your forehead or the back of your neck.
  • Keep caffeine under 200 mg a day from all sources.
  • Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is the pain reliever to use in pregnancy (see Section 6). Do not take ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin, or migraine medicine unless your provider tells you to.

Call your provider right away if

  • Your headache is severe, starts suddenly, gets worse, or does not get better with rest, fluids, and acetaminophen
  • You also have blurry vision, flashing lights or spots, dizziness, swelling of the face or hands, pain in the upper belly, nausea, or high blood pressure. These can be signs of preeclampsia, especially after 20 weeks.
  • You have fever, a stiff neck, weakness, numbness, confusion, trouble speaking, or you pass out
  • It is "the worst headache of your life": get emergency care

• Stretch your calf: straighten your leg and pull your toes toward you. Do this before bed.
  • Stay active with exercise your provider approves. Drink plenty of water. Wear comfortable, supportive shoes.
  • Massage the muscle, or use gentle heat.
  • Ask your provider before taking magnesium, calcium, or other supplements for cramps.

Call your provider if

  • Cramps are severe or frequent, or stretching does not help
  • One leg becomes swollen, red, warm, or tender
  • Leg pain comes with chest pain or trouble breathing: get emergency care

s6.title: What Medicines Can I Take If…
s6.intro: The medicines below are generally safe in pregnancy. Use the lowest dose that helps, and follow the package directions. Check with our office before you start any medicine, supplement, or herbal product that is not listed here.

items.h:
• First: avoid trigger foods, eat smaller meals, raise the head of your bed, and do not eat late at night.
  • Tums (calcium carbonate)
  • Maalox or Mylanta (magnesium hydroxide and aluminum hydroxide)
  • Pepcid AC or Zantac 360 (famotidine)
  • Prilosec (omeprazole) or Prevacid (lansoprazole), if antacids and famotidine are not enough

DO NOT TAKE: antacids with aspirin (such as Alka-Seltzer Original) or sodium bicarbonate.

• Fiber supplements: Metamucil (psyllium), Benefiber, Citrucel (methylcellulose)
  • MiraLAX (polyethylene glycol)
  • Colace (docusate sodium)
  • Milk of Magnesia (magnesium hydroxide), once in a while
  • Lactulose (prescription)

DO NOT TAKE: Pepto-Bismol (bismuth subsalicylate).

• Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) 10–25 mg every 6–8 hours
  • Doxylamine (Unisom SleepTabs) 12.5 mg (half of a 25 mg tablet) at bedtime, with vitamin B6. It can be repeated up to 3–4 times a day if needed. It can make you sleepy.
  • Ginger 250 mg capsule, up to 4 times a day
  • If these are not enough, call our office. Prescription medicines are available.

• Gas-X or Mylicon (simethicone)
  • Add fiber slowly. Avoid fizzy drinks and foods that give you gas.

DO NOT TAKE: Pepto-Bismol (bismuth subsalicylate).

items.t: I have allergies or a stuffy nose
items.h:
• Chlor-Trimeton (chlorpheniramine)
  • Claritin (loratadine)
  • Zyrtec (cetirizine)
  • Steroid nasal spray, such as Flonase (fluticasone)
  • Saline nasal spray or rinse

DO NOT TAKE pseudoephedrine (Sudafed and many "-D" products) in the first 3 months of pregnancy. It has been linked to a small risk of belly-wall birth defects. Check with our office before taking any other cold or cough medicine.

items.t: I have a headache or fever
items.h:
• Tylenol (acetaminophen), regular strength (325 mg) or extra strength (500 mg). Acetaminophen is the safest first choice for pain and fever in pregnancy. Use the lowest dose that works, for the shortest time needed. Follow the package directions for the daily limit.

DO NOT TAKE: ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), or aspirin unless your provider prescribes it. (Low-dose aspirin is sometimes prescribed to help prevent preeclampsia.)

s7.title: Planning for Birth: How Your Baby May Be Born
s7.intro: Our goal is a safe vaginal birth for you and your baby. Vaginal birth is the healthiest way to give birth for most patients, and it is what ACOG recommends unless there is a medical reason for a cesarean. Our team works to avoid cesareans that are not needed, especially a first cesarean, because that first surgery shapes every pregnancy after it. Your care team will talk with you about what is safest for you, and your wishes are part of that plan.

items.h:
Vaginal birth is how most babies are born, and it is the safest choice for most patients.

Why vaginal birth matters

  • Faster recovery. Most patients go home in 1–2 days and are back to normal activity sooner. There is no surgical wound to heal.
  • Fewer risks for you. Less bleeding, and lower risk of infection, blood clots, and injury to the bladder or bowel than with cesarean.
  • Safer future pregnancies. Each cesarean raises the risk of serious placenta problems (placenta previa and accreta), a scar that opens in labor, and hysterectomy in later pregnancies. A vaginal birth avoids these risks.
  • Better start for your baby. Babies born vaginally have fewer breathing problems after birth and can start skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding right away.
  • More choices next time. After a vaginal birth, you can plan a vaginal birth again without the limits that follow a cesarean.

What helps you have a vaginal birth

  • Letting labor start on its own when you and your baby are healthy. If labor needs to be started (induced) for a medical reason, your provider will explain why.
  • Having someone with you for support during labor, such as a partner, family member, or doula. Continuous support in labor lowers the chance of a cesarean.
  • Being patient. Early labor can take many hours. This is normal. You may be asked to stay home until labor is active.
  • Moving around and changing positions during labor.
  • Pain relief is your choice. An epidural does not raise your chance of a cesarean.

Near the end of labor, your provider may use a soft vacuum cup on the baby's head to help guide your baby out. This may be done if pushing is not moving the baby, or if the baby's heart rate shows the baby needs to be born quickly. About 3 in 100 U.S. births are assisted this way. Your provider will explain the reason and the small risks (such as bruising on the baby's scalp or a tear for you) first.

Most babies turn head-down by 36 weeks. If your baby is breech (bottom-first) at 36–37 weeks, your provider may offer to turn the baby by pressing on your belly (external cephalic version, or ECV). It works about half the time. If the baby stays breech, a planned cesarean is usually recommended.

A cesarean is major surgery. The baby is born through a cut in your belly and uterus. About 1 in 3 babies in the U.S. is born by cesarean; ACOG considers this rate too high. Some cesareans are planned before labor. Others are needed during labor. When a cesarean is medically needed, it is the safest choice.

Common reasons

  • Labor is not progressing, or the baby does not move down with pushing
  • The baby's heart rate shows the baby is not handling labor well
  • The baby is breech or sideways; twins or more, depending on position
  • The placenta covers the cervix (placenta previa)
  • A prior cesarean or uterine surgery, in some cases, or certain health conditions

What to know

  • Cesarean is safe, but it is major surgery. Risks include infection, bleeding, blood clots, injury to the bladder or bowel, and reactions to anesthesia.
  • Most patients stay in the hospital 2–4 days. Full recovery takes about 6 weeks.
  • A cesarean without a medical reason is not planned before 39 weeks. If you are thinking about asking for a cesarean, talk with your provider about the benefits and risks for you.

If you had a cesarean before, you may be able to have a vaginal birth this time. This is called VBAC (vaginal birth after cesarean). Trying for a VBAC is called a trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC).

  • Most patients with one prior cesarean with a low (transverse) cut on the uterus are candidates. Your provider will review your surgery records.
  • About 60–80 out of 100 patients who try for a VBAC have a vaginal birth. Success is more likely if you have had a vaginal birth before and if labor starts on its own.
  • The main risk is that the old scar opens during labor (uterine rupture). With a low cut, this happens in fewer than 1 in 100 labors. It is an emergency, so TOLAC is done in a hospital that can perform a cesarean right away, like Holy Name.
  • You can have an epidural during a TOLAC.
  • VBAC is not an option if you had a vertical ("classical") cut on the uterus or a prior uterine rupture.

Whether to try for a VBAC or plan a repeat cesarean is your decision, made with your provider. Talk about it early in pregnancy.

s9.title: Breastfeeding Basics

items.h:
• Breast milk is the ideal food. It changes as your baby grows. It is easier to digest than formula.
  • Antibodies in breast milk help your baby fight infection.
  • Breastfed babies have a lower risk of asthma, allergies, ear infections, stomach infections, obesity, and sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).

• Helps your uterus shrink back to its normal size. Reduces bleeding after birth.
  • May help you lose weight after birth.
  • Lowers your risk of breast cancer, ovarian cancer, type 2 diabetes, and high blood pressure.
  • It is convenient. Milk is always ready and at the right temperature.

• Any amount of breastfeeding helps.
  • Ideally, give only breast milk for the first 6 months.
  • Keep breastfeeding along with solid foods for 2 years or longer, as long as you and your baby want.

• 8–12 times in 24 hours in the early weeks. That is about every 2–3 hours.
  • Many newborns nurse for 10–15 minutes on each breast. Longer is normal too.
  • Feed your baby when you see hunger signs. Let your baby set the pace.

• Most newborns are ready to breastfeed within the first hour after birth.
  • Skin-to-skin contact right after birth helps your baby start feeding.
  • Keeping your baby in your room (rooming in) helps you learn your baby's signals and feed on demand.

• If breastfeeding is not possible or not right for you, that is OK. Your provider can help you choose what works for your family.
  • Our lactation consultants, nurses, and peer counselors are here to support you.
  • Breastfeeding classes are available at Holy Name.

s9.title: Breastfeeding Positions

items.h:
Breast milk has the right nutrients, in the right amounts, to feed your baby fully. Find a comfortable position. Bring your baby to your breast, not your breast to the baby. Use pillows or folded blankets for support.

Cradle hold

Sit up straight. Cradle your baby in the bend of your arm. Turn your baby's whole body toward you, belly to belly. Your baby's head rests in the bend of your elbow, facing your breast.

Football (clutch) hold

Tuck your baby under your arm like a football, at your side, level with your waist, facing you. Support your baby's back with your arm. Hold your baby's head level with your breast. This hold is helpful after a cesarean birth or if you have larger breasts.

Cross-cradle hold

Like the cradle hold, but you hold your baby with the opposite arm. If your baby is on your right breast, hold your baby with your left arm. Your baby's bottom rests in the bend of your elbow. Your hand supports the head and neck. This gives you more control of the head. It is good for a newborn who is having trouble latching.

Side-lying position

Lie on your side. Place your baby next to you, facing your breast. Put your fingers under your breast and lift it to help your baby reach the nipple. Rest your head on your lower arm. A pillow behind your back helps. This is good for night feedings and after a cesarean birth, because it keeps your baby's weight off your incision.

• Hold your breast in your hand. Stroke your baby's lower lip with your nipple. This makes your baby turn toward the nipple, open wide, and latch.
  • When your baby's mouth opens wide, pull your baby in close. Aim the nipple toward the roof of the mouth. The mouth should cover the nipple and much of the dark area around it (the areola). The lips should turn out.
  • Bring your baby to your breast, not your breast to your baby.
  • You should feel tugging, not pinching or pain. If it hurts, gently break the suction with a clean finger and try again.
  • Ask a nurse or lactation consultant for help before you leave the hospital.

s9.src: Sources: ACOG, Breastfeeding Your Baby (FAQ); ACOG Committee Opinion No. 820, Breastfeeding Challenges (2021).

s9.title: How Do I Know My Baby Is Hungry?
s9.intro: Crying is a late sign of hunger. Learn the early signs. Feeding your baby before crying starts makes latching easier for both of you.

items.t: Early signs of hunger: the best time to feed
items.h:
• Stirring, stretching, and moving more
  • Rooting: turning the head from side to side, or toward anything that touches the cheek, looking for the breast
  • Opening and closing the mouth, or making sucking motions
  • Licking the lips or sticking the tongue out
  • Putting hands or fists to the mouth again and again
  • Nuzzling against your breast when you hold your baby

items.t: Late signs of hunger: calm your baby first
items.h:
• Crying
  • Frantic or upset movements
  • Trouble settling down or latching

Calm your baby before you feed. Hold your baby skin-to-skin. Rock gently and talk softly. A very upset baby may have trouble latching.

• Watch your baby, not the clock. Every baby has their own feeding pattern.
  • Breastfed newborns usually nurse 8–12 times in 24 hours. That is about every 2 to 3 hours, counting from the start of one feeding to the start of the next.
  • In the early weeks, do not let your baby go more than about 4 hours without feeding. If your baby is sleepy or is not gaining weight well, gently wake your baby to feed.
  • Signs your baby is getting enough milk: at least 6 wet diapers a day by the end of the first week, regular bowel movements, and steady weight gain at your baby's checkups.
  • Hunger signs look different in every baby. You will learn your baby's signals over time.
